item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD(P)-binding occurs in several unrelated structural lineages, so it has evolved convergently multiple times; for example, SCOPe separates the Rossmann-like NAD(P)-binding fold c.2 from other cofactor-binding folds such as c.3. Divergent evolution is supported only within a family or, more remotely, a superfamily when the proteins share a broader conserved structural core and other homology evidence. NAD/NADP imposes similar chemical and geometric constraints, so unrelated enzymes can independently acquire similar glycine-rich loops, phosphate-binding features, cofactor orientations, or catalytic residues. Such local similarities are therefore analogies and cannot establish common ancestry, especially across different SCOPe folds. Homology should instead be evaluated using significant sequence similarity, whole-domain topology and structural alignment, conserved-core residue patterns, domain architecture, and phylogenetic evidence. Cofactor or active-site resemblance alone also does not justify transferring substrate specificity, reaction mechanism, or biological function. Likewise, a modeling template or representative should be selected from the appropriate homologous family or superfamily—with compatible domain boundaries, architecture, and function—not merely because it binds NAD(P) or has a locally similar active site.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
